x: Command Center The Command Center is the app for using an IntoMind One from your computer. It runs a small server on your computer and shows its page in your browser, where you connect to the device, watch the signal, record, and export. Then open http://localhost:8080. It needs Python 3.11 or newer. The page also works with no device connected, so you can review recordings anywhere. On Linux, ./install-launcher.sh adds it to your applications.

What it does Lists the devices it hears and connects only the one you pick. It shows the device's firmware, channels and protocol version. Shows the live signal, and which electrodes are in contact when lead-off detection is on. Records, with markers or with cued protocols such as eyes open and closed, blinks, jaw clenches and eye movements. Reads recordings back, runs analyses on them, and exports them. Selects a head on the device and shows its predictions, sets how often the model runs, and saves the model's embeddings to a file for training heads. Sets the status light and the device's name, and makes the device identify itself. Says above the trace whenever the signal does not come from the electrodes, and when another program on the computer is also listening to the device. The page has three levels. Basic shows every setting and lets you change a few everyday ones. Intermediate also lets you change the device's settings and its processing chain, and shows the ADC's registers. Advanced also lets you change the signal source and the analysis settings.

Recordings Recordings are saved in the captures folder inside the Command Center's folder, and exports in exports . A recording holds its samples, its events, and a record of how it was made: the device and its firmware, its settings, the processing chain, whether the signal was measured or generated, and where any gaps are. Checksums are written last, so a recording that stopped partway is never mistaken for a complete one.

Exports Format BDF 24-bit biosignal format, every value kept EDF the older 16-bit format, rounded to 16 bits npz NumPy arrays CSV and TSV text tables MATLAB version 7.3 files, every value kept Each export reports whether every value came out exactly as recorded, and if not, the largest error in microvolts. A recording whose checksums do not match is not exported. The Command Center uses the Python API's exporters, so a file exported here matches one exported from a script. In BDF and EDF every sample stays at the time it was recorded. Where samples were lost, the file fills the hole with a placeholder that repeats the last recorded value and labels it BAD_ACQ_SKIP , which MNE reads as a gap, and the page says how many samples it filled. A program that does not know the label shows a hole as a flat line. These files are made of whole blocks of about a second, and the last block is completed after the last sample the same way, so no recorded sample is left out, and the page says how many placeholders that took. What every file holds and promises is on Recordings and files . Every format carries electrode contact where detection was on during the recording, and only there, because a reading of "attached" means nothing when nothing was checking. CSV and TSV add a column per channel: 1 where the electrode was off, 0 where it was attached, and empty where detection was off. BDF and EDF label each stretch an electrode was off BAD_LEADOFF , which MNE treats as bad. The page says whether contact was checked. A recording made before this was kept says it is not known.

It answers only your computer The server listens only on your own computer, and it refuses requests from web pages on other sites, so a page you visit cannot reach it. The page loads nothing from the internet.

The device IntoMind One (IM-1)

What is in the box The IntoMind One, assembled and programmed, in its 3D printed enclosure, with its rechargeable battery and comfort strap. A T-shirt in the size you chose at checkout. A charging cable is not included.

Charging To ensure safety, never wear the device or touch its electrodes while USB is plugged in. Plug a USB-C cable into any USB charger or computer. The charge light shows what the charger is doing. Charging from empty takes about an hour and three quarters, and a full charge streams for about 25 hours. While USB is plugged in, the device charges and stays connected, but it does not stream from its electrodes. A stream cannot be started, and a stream that is running stops when the cable goes in. The synthetic signal still streams.

Turning it on and off Slide the power switch to turn the device on. The amber power light is lit while the device is on, and your computer can find it. The battery drains slowly even while the device is off, so charge it before you store it.

Wearing it The electrodes must touch skin, not hair. Part the hair where each electrode sits, and press the device down until the electrodes rest on the scalp. The comfort strap holds it in place and lets you place the electrodes anywhere on the head. It should feel firm but not tight. A noisy channel almost always means poor contact. Lift the device, part the hair again, and press it back down. If every channel is noisy, check the reference electrode. The Command Center can turn on lead-off detection, which shows which electrodes are in contact with the skin. It passes a very small current through the electrodes, so it stays off until you turn it on.

The lights Light Color What it shows Power amber lit while the device is on Charge yellow, magenta or red lit only while USB is plugged in: yellow while charging, magenta when full, red when no battery is connected Status amber what the device is doing, in the patterns below The status light has three settings: silent, reserved and verbose. The device ships set to reserved and keeps its setting when it is turned off. The Command Center sets it under the device's settings. Pattern Meaning Shown in Lit, with a short dark wink once a second your software asked this device to identify itself every setting Three blinks, then a pause the ADC failed its check at power on, so the device cannot record reserved and verbose Two blinks, then a pause the battery is below 20 percent, until it reaches 25 percent or USB is plugged in reserved and verbose Fast blinking an update is being written verbose A brief pulse every two seconds streaming verbose Steady connected verbose A short blink once a second on, and waiting for a computer verbose When more than one applies, the light shows the one highest in the table.

Connecting Turn the device on and connect from the Command Center or your own software. The first time, your computer pairs with the device, with no code to enter. After that it connects without pairing again. The link is encrypted. The device remembers four computers. When a fifth pairs, it forgets the one used least recently.
Several devices at once One computer can stream from two devices at 250 samples per second each. At 500 or 1000 samples per second, stream from one device per computer.

Its name The device can carry a name and an adjective that you choose, and every computer and phone that scans for Bluetooth devices sees them with the product's name: Ada's Blue IntoMind One. With only a name it is Ada's IntoMind One, with only an adjective Blue IntoMind One, and with neither IntoMind One. The device keeps them when it is turned off, and a new name appears in scans once the computer that set it disconnects. The whole name is at most 29 bytes. English letters, digits and spaces take one byte each. Accented letters and other scripts take two to four. When two devices near your computer have the same name, the software numbers the second one: Ada's IntoMind One 2. The number exists only on your computer.

The synthetic signal The device can stream a signal it generates itself, in place of its electrodes, to test software without anyone wearing it and for demonstrations. It runs at 500 samples per second, and every packet and recording of it is marked as generated. The Command Center says so above the trace. The device runs one neural network at a time. While it generates the signal, it sends no embeddings and no predictions, and it does not start generating while either is on. The generator draws the encoder's tokens, and the reconstruction head turns them back into signal. Compared with 19,459 windows of real EEG from 37 studies it was not trained on: Synthetic Real EEG A linear classifier on the encoder's embeddings, telling generated from real (0.5 means it cannot tell) 0.56 0.38 to 0.58, between real studies The same classifier, trained and scored on studies the generator never saw 0.64 A nonlinear classifier on the same embeddings 1.00, it always tells them apart Power spectrum, 1 to 45 Hz 1.5 dB from real EEG on average Coherence between channels, 8 to 13 Hz 0.18 0.28 The generator was trained with the encoder in the loop, so the first result is partly by design. The signal describes no one and varies less over time than a real person does. Use it to test software, never as data.

Firmware updates Firmware updates install over Bluetooth. The device keeps two copies of its firmware, writes an update to the copy it is not running, and runs only firmware signed by IntoMind. If your computer cannot connect after an update, turn the device off and on. If it still cannot connect, turn it off and on once more, and the device returns to the previous firmware.

If something is wrong What you see What to do It does not appear in a scan Check that the power light is on. If it is not, charge the device. One channel is noisy Improve that electrode's contact: lift the device, part the hair, and press it down. Every channel is noisy Improve the reference electrode's contact. A stream will not start, or stops Unplug USB. The device does not stream from its electrodes while USB is plugged in. It disconnects Move the computer closer, and away from other devices on the same radio band. It connects but never answers, or a feature is missing after an update Remove the device in your computer's Bluetooth settings (on Linux, bluetoothctl remove and its address) and connect again. Three blinks Turn the device off and on. If it happens again, write to support@intomind.com. The Command Center says another program is listening Another program on this computer is subscribed to the device, so every packet arrives twice. The copies are dropped and the recording is complete.

Recordings and files Every recording made with the Command Center or the Python API is kept the same way, and every export is written by the same code, whichever program asked for it. This page is the contract: what a recording is, what each file holds, and what will not change.

A recording A recording is a set of files that share one name, in the recordings folder ( captures by default). File What it holds name.npz The samples, as the converter's own counts for every channel, with each sample's index, device time and host time, and the lead-off byte and gap mark that arrived with it. name.meta.json The manifest: when the recording was made, the device and its firmware, its settings, the processing chain, whether the signal was measured or generated, where any gaps are, the electrode positions when they were given, and a version number for the manifest itself. name.events.json The markers placed during the recording, each at its device time. name.sha256 A checksum of every file above, written last. Four things hold for every recording: The checksums are written last. A recording without them stopped partway, and no export or analysis treats it as complete. A recording is never rewritten. A fact learned later, such as where the electrodes were, is kept in a separate file beside it, so what the instrument recorded and what a person added afterwards stay distinguishable. A manifest field is never renamed, and every older manifest version stays readable. New fields are added and old ones keep their meaning. The samples are the record. Every other file, including every export, is derived from them and can be made again.

Exports Six formats, one call. Every one refuses a recording whose checksums do not match. Every one reports the same six things, label , path , format , channels , samples and sample_rate_hz , and whether every value came out exactly as recorded. Where a value could not, lossy is true and max_error_uv is the largest error in microvolts. Format What it holds npz Microvolts per channel as ch1_uv and so on, with each sample's index, device time, host time, lead-off byte and gap mark, and the manifest. Every value as recorded. csv and tsv One header row, then one row per sample: host_time_s , device_time , and a microvolt column per channel. The rows are the samples, in order, and nothing is inserted where samples were lost. Both clocks are there so that a gap shows in the text. mat MATLAB version 7.3, which needs h5py . The microvolts as uv , the manifest, and the per-sample arrays. Every value as recorded. bdf BDF+, 24 bits per sample. At 24 bits the step is narrower than one converter count on any recording that does not span the whole converter, so the values are what was recorded and the error is measured, not assumed. edf EDF+, 16 bits per sample, and therefore lossy by construction. max_error_uv says by how much. The step depends on the signal's own range in the file, not on its offset. A recording the device generated is marked as generated wherever it goes: the columns are named ch1_synthetic_uv , the MATLAB matrix synthetic_uv , and the manifest says so.

x: Time in BDF and EDF files In BDF and EDF, every sample is written at the time it was recorded, counted from the sample index the device gave it. This is what the files promise, and what changed in 1.4.1. A hole holds one placeholder for every sample that was lost, so everything after it stays where it belongs, under a BAD_ACQ_SKIP annotation over exactly the hole. That is the label MNE gives a hole in its own files: it filters each side of a hole separately, rejects an epoch that overlaps one, and returns the hole as NaN when asked with get_data(reject_by_annotation="NaN") . A reader that does not know the label shows a hole as a flat line. The placeholder repeats the last recorded value, which is what MNE's own writer puts in the block it completes. These formats hold whole numbers, so NaN cannot be written. A value apart from the signal, such as the lowest number the file can store, is a step thousands of microvolts deep that a filter or a spectrum takes for signal. The last value adds no step and costs no precision, because it is already inside the signal's range. The last block. The files are whole blocks of about a second, and the last block is completed after the last sample with the same placeholder under the same label, so no recorded sample and no marker is left out. Before 1.4.1, the samples after the last whole block were left out of the file and counted in samples_dropped . That key is still reported, and is now 0. A restart. A recording whose sample count starts again within its first second begins with samples from before the recording started. The file starts at the restart, and samples_before_restart says how many samples were left out. A count that steps back later is a break whose length is not known, and the file is refused rather than given a timeline the recording does not have. The sample rate is kept exactly. The device's measured rate is rarely a whole number, and these formats need a whole number of samples per block, so the block's duration carries the remainder. The range each signal states in the header is rounded outward, so its lowest and highest samples are never clipped. Markers are written as annotations at their recorded times. What these two exports report, beyond the six things every export reports: Key Meaning gaps how many holes the file has samples_filled how many placeholders fill them tail_filled how many placeholders complete the last block samples_before_restart how many samples before a restart were left out samples_dropped how many recorded samples were left out of the file, 0 since 1.4.1 continuity +C for a continuous file bits , quantum_uv , lsb_uv the sample width, the file's step in microvolts, and the recording's own step

Lead-off in files Lead-off detection reports which electrodes have come off, and it runs only when it is turned on. A lead-off reading of zero means every electrode was attached only while detection ran, so every file carries lead-off only where the recording says detection was running, and says so. On the IntoMind One each channel's bit is its positive electrode. npz and mat carry the lead-off byte for every sample and, beside it, whether detection was running at that sample. csv and tsv add a column per channel, ch1_leadoff and so on, with 1 where the electrode was off, 0 where it was attached, and empty where nothing was checking. The columns are present only when detection ran somewhere in the recording. bdf and edf label each stretch an electrode was off BAD_LEADOFF followed by the channel's label, which MNE treats as bad, and label the part of a recording where detection was off LEADOFF_NOT_CHECKED , written only when it ran for the rest. every export reports contact : checked , partly checked , not checked , or not known for a recording made before the flag was kept. bdf and edf also report electrode_off_stretches .

Versions The Python package, the Rust crates and the JavaScript package share one version number. Its minor digit follows the minor version of the protocol, so a package that speaks protocol 1.4 is a 1.4 release. Its last digit counts releases of the packages. A name that has been published, whether a function, a key in a summary, a column in a file or a field in a manifest, keeps its meaning in every later release. New names are added, old names are never removed or renamed. This site describes the released packages, and nothing newer.

Glossary Term Meaning ADC The analog-to-digital converter, which turns the electrodes' voltages into numbers. The IntoMind One uses a Texas Instruments ADS1299-4. API The Python package intomind , for scripts, recordings and analysis. Capability A feature a device reports that it supports. Software asks a device only for what it reports. Channel One electrode, measured against the reference. The IntoMind One has four. Command Center The app for using the device from your computer, in your browser. Device time The device's own clock, which stamps every sample. Software maps it onto your computer's clock. Embedding The 76 numbers the encoder produces for each window. Heads read them. Encoder The neural network on the device that produces embeddings and tokens. Filter A high-pass filter removes slow drift, a low-pass filter removes fast content, and a notch filter removes a narrow band, such as the mains frequency. Gain How much the ADC amplifies the signal before converting it, from 1 to 24. Gap A place in a stream where samples were lost. The stream says where and how many. Generator The small model on the device that produces the synthetic signal. Head A small set of weights that turns an embedding into up to 32 numbers. You train heads and run them on the device. Lead-off detection A check that shows which electrodes touch the skin, by passing a very small current through them. Mains frequency The frequency of household electricity, 50 or 60 Hz, which every EEG picks up. Pairing The first connection between a computer and the device, which sets up the encryption for every later one. Placeholder A value written in a BDF or EDF file where a sample was lost, repeating the last recorded value, under the label that marks the hole. Processing chain The filters the device applies to its signal before streaming it. Every stream states its chain. Protocol The contract for the Bluetooth messages between an IntoMind device and any software. Reconstruction head The open head that turns tokens back into signal. Recording The samples, the manifest, the markers and the checksums that one capture session wrote, kept together under one name. Reference The electrode every channel is measured against. Sample One measurement of every channel at one moment. Sample rate How many samples the device takes per second: 250, 500 or 1000. SDK The Rust crates and the JavaScript package for building your own applications. Slot One of four places on the device for a head you upload. Synthetic signal A signal the device generates in place of its electrodes, marked as generated wherever it goes. Token One of the 80 vectors the encoder produces for each window, one per channel for each fifth of a second. Web Bluetooth The browser feature that lets a web page connect to a Bluetooth device. Window Four seconds of signal, the span the model describes at once. µV A microvolt, one millionth of a volt. EEG is measured in microvolts.

IntoMind ™ One IntoMind One is a research grade EEG device that you wear. It streams four channels of your brain's electrical activity to your computer over Bluetooth, and the software that records, analyzes and builds on it is open.

How it works Electrodes ADC Device clock Processing Bluetooth Encoder Generator 4 channels and a shared reference 24 bits, 250, 500 or 1000 per second every sample stamped with the device's time high-pass, mains notches, low-pass, by default encrypted, to your computer 76 numbers for each 4 seconds a synthetic signal, in place of the ADC The signal from the scalp to your computer Four electrodes and a reference rest on the scalp. The ADC converts what they pick up into 24-bit samples, at 250, 500 or 1000 samples per second, and the device stamps each sample with its own clock. The device filters the signal through a processing chain you can read and change, and every stream states the chain that produced it. If a sample is lost on the way, the stream says where and how many. Nothing is filled in. The device also runs a neural network that describes every 4 seconds of signal with 76 numbers. You can train heads on those numbers and run them on the device. In place of the electrodes, a generator on the device can stream a synthetic signal, marked as generated wherever it goes.

Try it With an IntoMind One switched on and unplugged, and a browser that has Web Bluetooth , you can connect to it from this page. Nothing is recorded, and nothing leaves your browser.

MicroPython MicroPython for the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, with the intomind library built in, lets a program on the board connect to an IntoMind One with no computer in the room. It is MicroPython 1.29.0 as released for the Pico 2 W with pairing added, because the IntoMind One accepts commands and sends data only over a paired, encrypted link, and MicroPython as released cannot pair on the Pico 2 W. Everything else MicroPython does on the board, Wi-Fi included, works as usual.

Install Download intomind-micropython-pico-2-w.uf2 from the firmware folder of github.com/intomind/micropython . Hold the BOOTSEL button while you plug the board into your computer, then let go. Drag the file onto the drive that appears. The board restarts into MicroPython, and its banner reads v1.29.0-intomind . In Thonny, choose MicroPython (Raspberry Pi Pico) at the bottom right, and the prompt is the board's. A program saved on the board as main.py runs whenever the board has power.

Connect and stream intomind.connect("Ada's") connects to the first device whose name starts with Ada's , and intomind.scan() lists every device heard, the strongest first. The first connection pairs the board with the device, and later connections reuse the pairing, which the board keeps in ble_secrets.json . If a connection fails because the device no longer has the pairing, the error says to call intomind.forget_pairings() , and the next connection pairs again. Each packet carries the index of its first sample. The next packet's index is this one's plus packet.n_samples , so a larger jump means samples were lost on the way. A stream started while the IntoMind One is plugged in is refused: start() raises intomind.Refused with status 7, because the device does not stream from its electrodes on USB power.

What the device reports The library holds no table of hardware. What a device can do is what it reports, and the methods for the battery, the model and heads raise OSError when it does not report that capability.

Run a head The IntoMind One runs heads on its own chip, and the board reads what they say. Train one in Python , or upload one from JavaScript . A program can then drive the board's pins from p.outputs , as a signal any circuit, robot or project of your own can act on.

Requests device.command(name, arg) sends any request in the protocol by name and returns what the answer carries. A refusal raises intomind.Refused , with the status number in status and its name in status_name . intomind.protocol is the protocol on its own, in plain Python, for reading what an answer carries, such as intomind.protocol.decode_battery(payload) . The library's tests read every message the way the published @intomind/sdk reads it.

The model and heads The IntoMind One runs a small neural network, an encoder, that reads 4 seconds of signal and describes it with 76 numbers, called an embedding. A head turns an embedding into the numbers you care about. You train heads on your own recordings, and the device runs them. ON THE DEVICE ON YOUR COMPUTER Window Encoder Tokens Embedding Head Reconstruction Signal 4 seconds of 4 channels, at 500 per second a small neural network, whose weights stay here 80 vectors, one per channel per fifth of a second 76 numbers, the mean of the tokens your weights, up to 32 outputs the open head: token to signal what the model kept of the window The encoder on the device, and the heads around it

Why it works this way The encoder was trained on EEG from many people and many studies, so it describes EEG in general. It knows nothing about you or your question. A head is where your question goes: a small set of weights, trained on a laptop in seconds, that reads the embedding and produces up to 32 numbers. The device then runs it on every window. A head is weights, never code. The device does not run code you send it.

What ships Every IntoMind One carries three open heads. Age is built into the model and selected when the device starts. Sex is in slot 1, one of the four slots that are yours. The reconstruction head is built into the model, where the device uses it for the synthetic signal . Age and sex show what an embedding carries. They are not useful predictors of either. The heads and how they were measured are published at github.com/intomind/eeg-foundation-model-heads .

Embeddings from the device The device sends the encoder's output on request while it streams, in two forms: The embedding , 76 numbers per window. Heads read it, so train heads on it. The tokens , 80 vectors per window, one per channel for each fifth of a second. The embedding is their mean, and they turn back into signal. Each window carries the index and device time of its first sample, so it lines up with your recording, and the identity of the encoder that produced it.

Training a head train_head fits a linear model with a ridge penalty that it chooses from your embeddings, and returns the head exactly as the device runs it. It refuses to fit unless there are more windows than the embedding has numbers. The embeddings you train on are the device's own, quantized as its heads receive them, so a head gives on your computer what it gives on the device.

Running it on the device The device checks a head's hash and its shape before it stores it. It never checks for a signature of ours, so you can run any head you train. A head records the encoder it was trained on, and the library and the Command Center warn you when it differs from the device's. Each prediction names the head that made it and the index of the window's first sample, so predictions line up with the signal. It also says whether the window had a gap or an electrode off. The model runs only on time the stream does not need, so it never costs you samples. The JavaScript and Rust packages upload heads too.

How often it runs By default the model describes every window, a new one every 4 seconds. You can ask for one window every so many seconds instead, on a grid that starts with the stream. The device keeps the setting when it is turned off.

What the model reads The model reads the stream: the processing chain's output, or the unfiltered signal when there is no chain. You can point it at the unfiltered signal or at a chain of its own without changing the stream, and every prediction says which it read. The model always works at 500 samples per second, from its own copy of the stream. The stream you receive is never resampled.

Turning tokens back into signal The open reconstruction head ships with the Python API and turns each token back into the fifth of a second it came from. What comes back is what the encoder kept of the window, in the model's normalized units. On windows from studies it was not fitted on, it returns about two thirds of the signal's variance: most of the rhythms below 13 Hz, less of those from 13 to 30 Hz, and little above 30 Hz. Windows with large artifacts do not come back in amplitude.

The weights The encoder's weights stay on the device. They arrive only in signed updates from IntoMind, cannot be read over the link, and are not published. Everything you work with is open: the embeddings and tokens the device sends, the heads you train, and the reconstruction head.

IntoMind BLE Protocol v1.0 Status: frozen 2026-09-19. This document is the contract between an IntoMind device and any host. Firmware, the api, the sdk, and the Command Center all implement it. Its canonical home moves to the api repository at publication.

0. Versioning and compatibility The device reports proto_major.proto_minor in Device Info. This document is 1.0. Within major version 1, a minor version only adds: new opcodes, new characteristics, new capability bits, new fields appended to Device Info. Nothing already defined changes meaning, size, or number. A 1.0 host works against every 1.x device by ignoring what it does not know. A major version change is allowed to break the wire format. The device advertises the major version so a host can refuse or adapt. Numbers that were used by any earlier firmware are never reused for a different meaning. Section 14 lists them. The wire formats of Device Info (first 27 bytes), EEG Data, the Control Point, and Status are byte for byte the v0.1 formats.

1. Design invariants On-device time is authoritative. Every sample carries a device time captured on the device, in hardware, at the converter's data-ready edge. The host maps device time onto its own clock. It never derives sample times from packet arrival. The timeline is never silently corrupted. A monotonic sample_index is the source of truth for continuity. Any loss is announced with an explicit discontinuity flag and count. The host reconstructs a timeline with marked holes, never a silent splice. The raw stream is never altered. The device acquires, timestamps, buffers, and streams the converter's samples unchanged. No filtering, scaling, or resampling happens on the raw stream. The on-device model of section 10 consumes a private copy of the stream and is additive: turning it on or off changes nothing about the raw data. The link is private. Data, control, status, and updates require an encrypted, bonded connection. Neural data belongs to its owner. The contract adapts to hardware. Capabilities and capacities are read from the device, so one contract serves devices with different channel counts, battery sensing, model presence, or slot sizes. The model can never hurt the instrument. Every model surface is optional. A device with no valid model behaves exactly like a device with no model at all, and acquisition never waits on inference.

3. Advertising and connection Advertising data: flags, complete list of 128-bit service UUIDs holding the service UUID. Scan response: complete local name IntoMind-1-XXXX , where XXXX is the last two bytes of device_id in uppercase hex. Multiple units are distinguishable before connecting. 5. EEG Data (notify) Header little-endian. The sample payload is the converter's own byte order: big-endian two's complement 24-bit integers, most significant byte first. The device copies converter bytes without per-sample swapping. The host sign-extends and scales. n_samples is at most the value set by SET_SAMPLES_PER_PACKET and never more than fits the negotiated MTU. One notification is one packet. Scaling on the host: microvolts = raw × (2 × vref_uv) / (gain × 2^24) . At gain 24 and a 4.5 V reference one count is about 0.02235 µV. Continuity on the host: the expected next sample_index is the previous packet's sample_index plus its n_samples . Compute step = new_index − expected as a signed 32-bit difference so the index's own wrap is exact. step == 0 and bit0 clear: continuous. step > 0 : step samples were lost. They span the corresponding device time range. samples_lost_before carries the same number when it fits in 16 bits. step <= 0 , or bit0 set with step == 0 : the timeline re-based (RESET_EPOCH or a stream start). This is a break, not a loss. The device sets bit0 and samples_lost_before = 0. A host must never turn a non-positive step into a loss count. Taking the unsigned difference here reports a loss that never happened. Every sample in an epoch is acquired under one configuration, because configuration changes are refused while streaming.

7. Status (read and notify) Notified on any state change and at about 1 Hz while connected. battery_percent is a state of charge estimate from the measured pack voltage on the IntoMind One. GET_BATTERY carries the voltage itself. loff_statp mirrors the per-packet value. Before the first sample of a session it reads 0. Use the per-packet copy for contact tracking. buffer_high_watermark is set while buffer_fill is at or above three quarters of the device's buffer. Read it as backpressure. dropped_total counts every sample acquired but never delivered: buffer overflow, conversions the acquisition path could not read in time, and anything discarded at an epoch boundary. Only a reboot clears it. It is telemetry. The authoritative account of what a host missed is sample_index continuity.

8. Time sync (informative) Device time is monotonic and free running. The converter's clock and the host's clock drift relative to each other by tens of parts per million, so a host that needs alignment better than about 10 ms re-syncs every few minutes: Note host time T1 , write TIME_SYNC. The device captures Td at receipt and returns it. Note host time T2 at the response. Estimate offset ≈ (T1+T2)/2 − Td with uncertainty ±(T2−T1)/2 . Regress offset over several syncs to estimate skew. Map any sample: host_time ≈ device_time × (1 + skew) + offset . Multiple devices each sync independently to the same host clock, which puts them on one timebase at millisecond alignment without wires.

9. Update service The Update service carries three kinds of transfer: an application image, a weights image, and a user head. Application and weights images are produced by IntoMind, signed, and encrypted. A host carries them as opaque bytes and needs no key. Heads are plain blobs in the format of section 11, made by anyone.

9.1 Rules A transfer is refused with status 3 while streaming. Stop the stream first. One transfer at a time. START while one is in progress is refused with status 3. ABORT ends it. The running application is never written. An application image goes to the idle slot. The device tells the host which slot that is, and the host sends the image variant built for that slot. A weights image is written in place. If power fails during the write the partition fails verification at the next boot, predictions are unavailable, and everything else works. A new weights transfer repairs it. A head is written to the slot named in START. Slot 0, the built-in head, cannot be written or removed. The device keeps a transfer's progress in memory across a disconnect. START with identical parameters resumes at the reported offset. A reboot starts over.

9.2 Update Control (write, indicate) Request [op, ...] , response [op, status, payload?] . Status codes: Code Meaning 0 OK 1 invalid argument or malformed request 2 unsupported (no such target on this device) 3 busy: streaming, or a transfer is already active 4 no transfer in progress 5 flash error 6 verification failed, see verify_result Operations: Op Command Request Response payload 0x01 START u8 target, u8 slot, u32 total_len, u8[8] transfer_id u8 target_slot, u16 chunk_max, u32 resume_offset 0x02 QUERY u8 state, u32 offset, u32 crc32 0x03 FINISH u8 verify_result 0x04 ACTIVATE 0x05 ABORT target : 1 application, 2 weights, 3 head. slot : for a head, 1..head_slots. Zero otherwise. total_len : the exact number of bytes the host will send. For images this is the envelope length (section 9.4). For a head it is the blob length. transfer_id : the first 8 bytes of the SHA-256 of the full transfer. The device uses it only to recognize a resume. target_slot : for an application, the slot that will receive the image, 0 = A or 1 = B. The host must send the variant linked for that slot. Zero for other targets. chunk_max : the largest Update Data write the device accepts. Equal to update_chunk_max in Device Info unless the MTU is smaller. resume_offset : bytes already accepted from an identical earlier START. The host continues from this offset. QUERY state : 0 idle, 1 receiving, 2 complete (FINISH verified), 3 failed. offset is the number of bytes accepted so far. crc32 is the IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 (the zlib CRC) over those bytes as sent, so a host can check it against its own copy without any key. FINISH verifies the whole transfer and answers status 0 with verify_result 0, or status 6 with the reason. After status 0 the transfer state is complete and ACTIVATE is allowed. ACTIVATE for an application: the device marks the new image for a trial boot, confirms the indication, then resets within one second. The link drops. If the new image fails to confirm itself, the bootloader returns to the previous image and GET_BOOT_INFO reports reason 6. ACTIVATE for weights: the device confirms the indication and then resets, the same way. Weights are verified at every boot, so restarting is what puts the new ones in force and what proves they are sound before anything runs on them. If they are not, the device comes back with predictions unavailable and everything else working. ACTIVATE for a head: status 2. A head is written and verified by FINISH and selected with SELECT_HEAD. verify_result : Value Meaning 0 verified 1 length differs from total_len 2 malformed envelope or image header 3 target mismatch between START and the image 4 slot mismatch: the image is linked for the other slot 5 content hash mismatch 6 signature invalid 7 image security counter is lower than the installed image's 8 head dimensions do not match this device 9 flash write failure 10 unknown key id

9.3 Update Data (write without response) Each write appends its bytes to the transfer. No framing, at most chunk_max bytes per write. The link layer delivers writes in order and without loss. A host paces itself with QUERY, for example every 32 writes, and compares offset and crc32 with its own count.

9.4 Image envelope An application or weights image travels inside an envelope whose first 32 bytes are plain and describe the payload. The remainder is encrypted and opaque to the host. A release of the application ships as two envelopes, one per slot_link . The host reads target_slot from START and sends the matching one. The device rejects a mismatch with verify_result 4 before any flash is written.

10. Predictions (notify) Model outputs, one notification per window. Present in the GATT table on every device with a model runtime. Notifications flow only while streaming, with predictions enabled, a ready model, and a selected head. The window is the window_samples raw samples starting at sample_index . A host aligns predictions to its recording through the same index it uses for the raw stream. The model consumes its own copy of the stream resampled to model_native_sps . At the native rate a window is model_window_samples raw samples. At 250 SPS it is half that. Each output is scale[o] × (bias[o] + Σ W[o][i] × e[i]) for the selected head (section 11). The host applies any activation it wants. Cadence is the device's choice within its compute budget. Windows are self describing, so a host never assumes a fixed hop. head_id names the head that produced the outputs. Recordings should store it with the predictions.

11. Heads A head is weights, never code. It maps the model's embedding to a small number of outputs. The embedding e is a vector of model_embed_dim signed 16-bit integers in units of 1/4096. The runtime computes the embedding in floating point and quantizes it at that fixed scale before running a head. The scale is part of this contract: changing it would change every head ever trained. The sdk runs the same runtime on the host and produces the same integers, which is what lets a head trained on a host behave identically on the device. Head blob, little-endian: head_id is the first 8 bytes of sha256 . On FINISH the device checks magic, version, kind, in_dim against its embedding width, out_dim against head_max_outputs , total length against the field sizes, and the hash. Any failure is verify_result 8 (dimensions) or 5 (hash) and nothing is stored. Slot 0 holds the built-in head that ships with the weights image. User slots are 1..head_slots. A head blob for the IntoMind One is at most head_slot_bytes , which the format satisfies at every allowed size. Removing or overwriting the active head deselects it. Predictions stop until SELECT_HEAD names another.

12. Security LE Secure Connections with bonding are required for every characteristic except Device Info. Pairing is Just Works. This defeats passive eavesdropping, which is the primary threat to neural data. It does not defend against an active attacker present during the initial pairing, which is the accepted limit of a device with no display or button. Update images are signed. The device installs nothing whose signature it cannot verify, and a running image never writes over itself. A failed new image rolls back automatically. Local first. No cloud dependency. Any network feature of a host application is opt in and never a precondition for using the device.

15. Conformance The reference codec for every message in this document is a small library that both the firmware and the host tooling build unchanged, so an encoder on one side and a decoder on the other are the same code. Its test vectors are the conformance suite for any independent implementation. A host implementation is conformant when it decodes every vector to the documented fields and refuses every malformed vector. The vectors are published as one JSON file, emitted by the firmware from the codec it runs. Every message kind in this document appears there, and so does a set of malformed messages for each kind, each with the reason it is refused: truncated, invalid, or reserved. Two rules govern the file itself, so that a reader in any language gets the same answer from it. A 64-bit field is written as a decimal string. A device time runs past what a JSON number holds exactly. A reader that parses one as a floating-point number lands a few ticks away, and it then agrees with an expectation that was rounded the same way, so the mistake passes unseen. Parse these as integers. A count that does not exist is written as null, never as zero. A break in the timeline has no extent, and zero there would claim that nothing was lost.

8. Time sync (informative) Device time is monotonic and free running. The converter's clock and the host's clock drift relative to each other by tens of parts per million, so a host that needs alignment better than about 10 ms re-syncs every few minutes: Note host time T1 , write TIME_SYNC. The device captures Td at receipt and returns it. Note host time T2 at the response. Estimate offset ≈ (T1+T2)/2 − Td with uncertainty ±(T2−T1)/2 . Regress offset over several syncs to estimate skew. Map any sample: host_time ≈ device_time × (1 + skew) + offset . Multiple devices each sync independently to the same host clock, which puts them on one timebase at millisecond alignment without wires.

9. Update service The Update service carries three kinds of transfer: an application image, a weights image, and a user head. Application and weights images are produced by IntoMind, signed, and encrypted. A host carries them as opaque bytes and needs no key. Heads are plain blobs in the format of section 11, made by anyone.

9.1 Rules A transfer is refused with status 3 while streaming. Stop the stream first. One transfer at a time. START while one is in progress is refused with status 3. ABORT ends it. The running application is never written. An application image goes to the idle slot. The device tells the host which slot that is, and the host sends the image variant built for that slot. A weights image is written in place. If power fails during the write the partition fails verification at the next boot, predictions are unavailable, and everything else works. A new weights transfer repairs it. A head is written to the slot named in START. Slot 0, the built-in head, cannot be written or removed. The device keeps a transfer's progress in memory across a disconnect. START with identical parameters resumes at the reported offset. A reboot starts over.

10. Predictions (notify) Model outputs, one notification per window. Present in the GATT table on every device with a model runtime. Notifications flow only while streaming, with predictions enabled, a ready model, and a selected head. The window is the window_samples raw samples starting at sample_index . A host aligns predictions to its recording through the same index it uses for the raw stream. The model consumes its own copy of the stream resampled to model_native_sps . At the native rate a window is model_window_samples raw samples. At 250 SPS it is half that. Each output is scale[o] × (bias[o] + Σ W[o][i] × e[i]) for the selected head (section 11). The host applies any activation it wants. Cadence is the device's choice within its compute budget. Windows are self describing, so a host never assumes a fixed hop. head_id names the head that produced the outputs. Recordings should store it with the predictions.

11. Heads A head is weights, never code. It maps the model's embedding to a small number of outputs. The embedding e is a vector of model_embed_dim signed 16-bit integers in units of 1/4096. The runtime computes the embedding in floating point and quantizes it at that fixed scale before running a head. The scale is part of this contract: changing it would change every head ever trained. The sdk runs the same runtime on the host and produces the same integers, which is what lets a head trained on a host behave identically on the device. Head blob, little-endian: head_id is the first 8 bytes of sha256 . On FINISH the device checks magic, version, kind, in_dim against its embedding width, out_dim against head_max_outputs , total length against the field sizes, and the hash. Any failure is verify_result 8 (dimensions) or 5 (hash) and nothing is stored. Slot 0 holds the built-in head that ships with the weights image. User slots are 1..head_slots. A head blob for the IntoMind One is at most head_slot_bytes , which the format satisfies at every allowed size. Removing or overwriting the active head deselects it. Predictions stop until SELECT_HEAD names another.

It does not defend against an active attacker present during the initial pairing, which is the accepted limit of a device with no display or button. Update images are signed. The device installs nothing whose signature it cannot verify, and a running image never writes over itself. A failed new image rolls back automatically. Local first. No cloud dependency. Any network feature of a host application is opt in and never a precondition for using the device.

Conformance The reference codec for every message in this document is a small library that both the firmware and the host tooling build unchanged, so an encoder on one side and a decoder on the other are the same code. Its test vectors are the conformance suite for any independent implementation. A host implementation is conformant when it decodes every vector to the documented fields and refuses every malformed vector. The vectors are published as one JSON file, emitted by the firmware from the codec it runs. Every message kind in this document appears there, and so does a set of malformed messages for each kind, each with the reason it is refused: truncated, invalid, or reserved. Two rules govern the file itself, so that a reader in any language gets the same answer from it. A 64-bit field is written as a decimal string. A device time runs past what a JSON number holds exactly. A reader that parses one as a floating-point number lands a few ticks away, and it then agrees with an expectation that was rounded the same way, so the mistake passes unseen. Parse these as integers. A count that does not exist is written as null, never as zero. A break in the timeline has no extent, and zero there would claim that nothing was lost.

Each stage runs in the converter's own count domain and the result is rounded back into twenty-four bits, so the scaling rule of section 5 applies unchanged, and the timestamp of a processed sample is the timestamp of the natural sample it corresponds to. 16.3 Defaults and persistence The chain is on from the first boot. The device's default is a 0.5 Hz high-pass, the mains bands the rate can represent (both mains fundamentals and their second and third harmonics, four hertz wide, until a host removes the ones that do not apply), and the automatic low-pass. The bands are 48 to 52, 58 to 62, 98 to 102, 118 to 122, 148 to 152 and 178 to 182 Hz. At 250 samples a second the last three reach past nine tenths of the Nyquist rate, 112.5 Hz, so the default there holds three bands. The automatic low-pass sits at 100, 200 and 400 Hz at 250, 500 and 1000 samples a second. A notch places its null at the middle of its band and runs as two sections, so mains 0.03 Hz off its nominal frequency is more than 60 dB down. The chain in force persists on the device across power cycles, so every host sees the same instrument. origin in GET_PIPELINE says whether the chain in force is the device's default, which the device recomposes at every rate change, or a host's, which binds the rate as section 6 describes.

The values are the chip's own, as its datasheet defines them; nothing in them is secret, and the protocol already reports the settings they encode. Read only. No register write exists in this contract and none will be added: a write could drive lead-off or bias current into the wearer or break the acquisition. The device reads the chip when asked. If the chip cannot be read in its current state, for example while it is converting continuously, the device either pauses the chip for the read without losing samples or answers status 3, and says which in its device page. The IntoMind One answers status 3 while streaming. It never answers from a copy of what it last wrote. The ADS1299 family carries 24 registers, addresses 0x00 to 0x17; the first is the chip's identity register, which names the exact part and its channel count. Embeddings A device that sets capability bit 12 runs its encoder on each window and sends the result to the host, in one of two forms: The window embedding : model_embed_dim numbers describing the whole window, the mean of the tokens below over the live channels and over time. 22. Synthetic signal A device that sets capability bit 16 holds, beside its encoder, a decoder that turns the encoder's tokens back into signal (the open reconstruction head for that encoder) and a generator, a small recurrent model over the encoder's token space trained on the corpus. The three travel together in the weights image, each named by its hash, and the device sets bit 16 only when the generator names the encoder and the decoder it was trained beside. In synthetic mode the converter is not driven. The device draws each channel's next token from the generator, one fifth of a second at a time, turns it into samples with the decoder, adds noise shaped by two fixed filters for what the decoder does not return, and streams the result at the stream's channel count with the stream's own timestamps, indices, and packet cadence. Nothing downstream of the converter is different: the chain, the buffer, gaps and packets run as they do on a measured signal. The foundation model does not run beside the generator (22.4).

22.1 Entering and leaving The status message's mode field reads 3 while the mode is in force. While it is, SET_RATE to any rate but 500 answers status 1 and changes nothing, and SET_MODE with a converter mode, 0, 1, or 2, leaves it.

22.2 The packet Synthetic samples are streamed as packet type 0x04 with exactly the layout of type 0x01 (section 5): the same header, the same sample encoding, the same flags and mode bits. A host decodes it with the code it has for 0x01 and knows every sample in it was generated. A 1.2 host, whose decoder refuses an unknown packet type, never stores one. Samples are in converter counts, as the device would have measured a signal of the amplitude the device page states, with the gain field filled in as usual, so a host scales them the way it scales everything. A slice the generator has not finished when its samples are due is never repeated or invented: the stream's index moves past it, and a host sees the gap as it sees any other.

s: 22.3 What it is and is not
x: 22.3 What it is and is not The synthetic signal reproduces what the generator learned: the corpus's power spectrum, band powers, and channel correlations, and the way one fifth of a second follows the last. It contains no events, because a decoder driven by statistics does not make blinks, spindles, or spikes. Its purpose is a stream with the device's real timing that needs no wearer: for building and testing software against the device, for demonstrations, and for sharing sessions that hold no one's brain data. What it matches and how well is measured and stated on the device page. Its realism is a property of the generator, which travels in the weights image and changes only with a signed weights update.

22.4 One model at a time The generator and the foundation model are two models, and a device runs one of them at a time. SET_MODE 3 is refused with status 3 while predictions are on or embeddings are asked for. While the mode holds, SET_PREDICTIONS on and SET_EMBEDDINGS with any form but off are refused with status 3, and off is always accepted. A pass of the foundation model begun before the mode was entered stops at its next step and its result is never sent. Only the generator excludes the converter: reconstructing signal from the tokens of acquired signal needs the converter and the foundation model, and not the generator. Input source 3, synthetic, stays defined for a reader, and a device that runs one model at a time never sends it. Not in 1.3: seeding the generator from live signal (the device embedding what it acquires and continuing from those tokens), and a host-supplied generator. Both are additions when wanted.

23. Weights update behavior The weights partition is single and is written in place, so from the first byte of a transfer the running model's weights are no longer whole. While a weights transfer (section 9, target weights) is in progress the model is therefore stopped before anything is written: GET_MODEL_INFO reports model state 3, updating; embeddings and predictions pause; the stream is unaffected. Activation of a verified weights image restarts the device, as it always has, and the restart is what puts the new weights in force: they are verified at boot as every image is, and the device comes back ready with the new encoder's identity and width. A transfer that is aborted, or fails to verify, leaves the model as it finds it: ready with the old weights if nothing was written to the partition yet, and otherwise state 1, no weights, until a restart puts verified weights in force. A host re-reads GET_MODEL_INFO after any weights transfer. Heads are handled as section 21 says.

The device's name A device that sets capability bit 17 composes its Bluetooth name from two strings a host may set, a name and an adjective, both kept across power cycles and both empty from the factory. The composed name is, in order and separated by single spaces: the name followed by 's , when a name is set; the adjective, when set; the product name, which for the IntoMind One is IntoMind One . So a device reads Ada's Blue IntoMind One , Blue IntoMind One , Ada's IntoMind One , or IntoMind One . A 1.2 device advertised IntoMind-1- and four hex digits; that form is gone. A host recognizes a device by the service identifier it advertises, never by its name, as it already did.

24.1 The whole name always fits The composed name is the device's Bluetooth device name and its complete local name in the air. A scan response carries at most 29 bytes of name, which is what every scan list on every phone and computer can show, so the composed name is limited to 29 bytes of UTF-8. The limit is on the result, not on the parts: a long name leaves less room for an adjective. A host computes the same bytes before sending and shows the user the room left. Nothing is ever shortened, and what a scan list shows is the whole name.

24.2 Reading and setting The parts are stored before the response is sent. The device advertises the composed name from the next time it advertises, which is after the host that set it disconnects. Its device name characteristic, which a host reads once connected, takes the new name at the next restart; a host that wants the two to agree at once sends SOFT_RESET after SET_NAME. A factory reset clears both parts. On a device without capability bit 17 both opcodes answer status 2.

A host that lists devices appends a number, starting at 2, to the second and later devices with the same composed name in that list, in the order heard, and drops it once the list holds no twin. The number is the host's alone, never sent to the device and never stored, and every host of ours renders it the same way.

25. USB power The IntoMind One is not worn while it is plugged in. From 1.4 the device holds to that itself: nothing that needs the device on someone's head runs while USB power is present. USB power is what Status reports as usb_present , flag bit 0.

25.1 What is refused While usb_present is set, START_STREAM answers status 7 unless the device is in the synthetic mode of section 22. That covers every mode that reads the converter: the natural signal from the electrodes (mode 0), the converter's own test signal (mode 1), and its shorted inputs (mode 2). The converter is not started. Electrode contact quality and everything the device computes from the natural signal ride on such a stream, so they do not run either. Settings are not refused: a host may choose a mode, a rate, a gain or a chain while plugged in, and they take effect on the next stream. Precedence, extending section 6 of 1.0: invalid argument, then unsupported, then busy, then USB power, then hardware.

25.2 What stops A stream of the natural signal that is running when USB power appears ends at once. Its last sample is the last one converted before the device saw USB power, and no sample after it is streamed. Samples already queued are still sent, and every packet sent after the device saw USB power carries usb_present , data flag bit 4, so a host can tell from the packets alone. The next Status message, within one second, reads state 0 with usb_present set, and that pair is the reason. A host tells its user to unplug to record. The samples streamed are complete and the stream simply ends, so there is no gap inside it to mark. The device does not resume when USB power goes away. A host starts a new stream.

25.3 What runs The synthetic signal of section 22 streams while plugged in, with its processing chain and the one model of section 22. So does everything that does not read the electrodes: the connection, Device Info, settings, the name, the lamp, updates, battery and charger state.

25.4 A 1.3 host A 1.3 host does not know status 7. Under section 0 of 1.1 it treats any status other than 0 as a refusal, so its user sees a stream that did not start, or one that ended, with usb_present set in the same Status.

27. Embedding notifications fit 156 bytes Section 3 of 1.0 holds every notification and indication but EEG Data to 156 bytes, so that an MTU of 159, the smallest the contract allows for them, carries each one whole. Section 19.2 of 1.2 said instead that an embedding notification carries as many values as fit the negotiated MTU, and that 96 values fit at that smallest MTU. The count is wrong: after the 28 byte header, 64 values fit. And firmware 1.2 to 1.4.1 kept neither rule. It filled a part with up to 108 values, 244 bytes, whatever the MTU, so the launch model's 76 value vectors each went as one notification of 180 bytes, which a host below an MTU of 183 received cut short. From 1.4, as built in firmware 1.4.2, an embedding notification carries at most 64 values, 156 bytes, on every link. A vector wider than that goes in parts exactly as section 19.2 of 1.2 defines: each part names its first value, and every part but the last sets more_parts . The launch model's vectors go in two parts, 64 values and 12. A host puts parts back together as it always has, so a 1.2 or 1.3 host reads them unchanged, and a notification from an earlier firmware reads as it did. No number is assigned, and nothing else changes.

Python The intomind package is the Python API for the IntoMind One. It connects to the device, streams its signal, and reads, exports and analyzes recordings. The Command Center is built on it. It needs Python 3.11 or newer. The analysis extra installs SciPy, which reading recordings, exporting and the analyses need. For MATLAB export, install 'intomind[analysis,mat]' . Each sample carries the device's index ( sample.index ), the device time at which it was converted ( sample.device_time ), that time on your computer's clock ( sample.host_time ), and one value per channel in microvolts ( sample.uv ). The first connection pairs the device with your computer, and later connections reuse the pairing. On Linux the library answers the pairing request itself, so no settings window is needed and a computer without a screen works. If a connection fails because the link could not be secured, the error says what to do.

What the device reports The library holds no table of hardware. What a device can do is what it reports, and a request for anything else is refused before it is sent, with an error that names the missing capability.

Processing on the device The device filters its signal through a chain you can read and change, and only the chain's output streams. The device refuses changes while it streams: stop, set, and start again. A chain that cannot run at the device's rate is refused, with the reason, before anything is sent.

Gaps and repeated packets The device numbers every sample, so a loss has an exact count. When the device restarts its count, the library reports a break of unknown length, never a count. Where recordings go Recordings go to ~/.local/share/intomind/captures unless INTOMIND_CAPTURES or use_captures_dir names another folder. use_site records facts about where you record. Anything you do not declare is recorded as unknown.

Exports Each export reports whether every value came out exactly as recorded, and if not, the largest error in microvolts. A recording whose checksums do not match is refused. In BDF and EDF, every sample stays at the time it was recorded. Where samples were lost, the file holds one placeholder for each of them, repeating the last recorded value, under a BAD_ACQ_SKIP annotation that MNE reads as its own, so MNE leaves the hole out of filtering and returns it as NaN when asked. A reader that does not know the label shows a hole as a flat line. The files are whole blocks of about a second, and the last block is completed after the last sample the same way, so no recorded sample is left out. export.export reports how many placeholders it wrote in samples_filled and tail_filled . What every file holds and promises is on Recordings and files . Lead-off is in every format, and only where the recording says detection was running, because a lead-off status of zero is an attached electrode there and nothing at all anywhere else. CSV and TSV add a chN_leadoff column per channel: 1 where the electrode was off, 0 where it was attached, and empty where nothing was checking. BDF and EDF label each stretch an electrode was off BAD_LEADOFF and the channel, which MNE treats as bad. NPZ and MATLAB hold the flag itself as leadoff_active . Every export reports in contact whether contact was checked, and a recording made before the flag was kept reports "not known".

Safety and care

Not a medical device The IntoMind One is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease or condition. It is a research and development instrument. Nothing it records or reports is a clinical measurement, and nothing on this site is medical advice. You use it at your own risk.

Who should not use it Infants, young children, and anyone with a weak or sensitive scalp. Anyone with an implanted electrical device, such as a pacemaker, a neurostimulator, or a cochlear implant, without first asking the doctor who manages it. Anyone with broken or irritated skin where the electrodes would rest.

While you wear it The device is designed to be safe against a single electrical fault on battery power only. To ensure safety, never wear it or touch its electrodes while USB is plugged in. Do not use it in wet or damp conditions, or while driving, operating machinery, or doing anything else where a distraction could cause harm. The electrodes only measure, except when you turn on lead-off detection, which passes a very small current through them. Take the device off if the skin under an electrode becomes sore or red.

The battery The device has a lithium polymer battery. Treat it as you would the battery in a phone. Charge it from an ordinary USB charger or computer. Do not charge it unattended on a soft surface. Do not puncture or crush the device. If the device becomes hot, swells, or smells, stop using it, move it away from anything that can burn, and do not charge it again. Do not put it in household waste. Take it to a battery recycling point.

Cleaning With the power off, charger disconnected, and ideally the battery disconnected as well, wipe the electrodes with a damp cloth and let them dry. Do not use solvents, alcohol or abrasives on them. Do not submerge the device or hold it under running water. It is not sealed.
Storage Store the device dry and charged. The battery drains slowly even while the device is off, and a lithium battery left empty for a long time may not recover.

Your recordings Recordings are written to your own computer. The Command Center and the Python API send nothing over the internet and need no account. A recording of brain activity is personal data, so share one only on purpose.
